summary:
Beyond the Fog: Project Summary
NASA missions have left scientific instruments, landers and rovers on the Moon and Mars. Each one marks a milestone in space exploration and carries a scientific and historical story, yet most people do not know why these objects were left behind.
This is a community problem, not only a scientific one. Information about these artifacts is scattered across many sources, written in technical language that young people struggle to follow, and rarely told as an interactive story. For Arabic speakers the gap is wider: almost everything available on the topic is in foreign languages, so Arab students are cut off from this part of human history.
Beyond the Fog is our answer: an interactive educational web experience that turns NASA’s open data into engaging digital stories for students aged 10–18, teachers and space enthusiasts. Users explore the space environment, select an artifact, discover its mission, scientific purpose and achievements, then test what they learned through interactive activities.
To close the language gap, we produced complete videos ourselves, designed by our team and narrated in our own voices, with original Arabic content.
Next, we plan to add more artifacts, 3D and augmented reality, more languages, and educational games.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Beyond the Fog is an interactive educational web experience that tells the stories of the machines humanity left on the Moon and Mars. The user opens a mission map, picks a mission (Moon or Mars), and moves through it level by level. Each level is dedicated to one artifact, for example the Apollo Lunar Modules, Falcon (Apollo 15), Intrepid (Apollo 12) and Surveyor 3 on the Moon, and Mars Pathfinder with its Sojourner rover on Mars. A level presents the artifact’s mission, launch and landing details, scientific purpose, achievements and current status, supported by an Arabic video, and ends with a short quiz. Passing the quiz earns experience points and unlocks the next level.

What benefits does it have?

- It gathers information that is scattered across many sources into one clear, organized place.

- It turns technical descriptions into short stories that a 10 to 18 year old can follow.

- It gives teachers a ready classroom resource, with a video and a quiz for every topic.

- It offers Arabic-speaking learners content in their own language, where almost everything on this topic is in foreign languages.

- Levels, points and quizzes turn passive reading into active learning and keep students motivated.

What is the intended impact?

We see the lack of accessible Arabic space content as a community problem, because language decides who gets to take part in science. Our aim is to give Arab students the same access to this part of human history as anyone else, to raise curiosity about space science and STEM careers, and to show that young people in our community can produce scientific content and not only consume it. In the longer term, we want these artifacts to be remembered as human heritage and not as forgotten equipment.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did we use?

- Data and images: NASA open sources, including the NASA Open Data Portal, NASA Science, the NASA Image and Video Library and the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive.

- Website: built with [HTML, CSS and JavaScript], with an Arabic right-to-left interface.

- Use of AI: we used Anthropic’s Claude model to assist in developing the website.

- Videos: produced entirely by our team, including design, editing and voice-over, using [video editing software] and [audio recording tool].

How is the project creative?

Instead of a list of facts, each artifact becomes a story the user travels through, on a map that feels like a game. The videos are original work in our own voices, which gives the project a human, local identity. Combining storytelling, gamification and original Arabic media around abandoned space artifacts is, as far as we know, a new approach for this audience.

What factors did the team consider?

- Accuracy: all scientific content comes from NASA sources.

- Age: simple language, short videos and only three questions per quiz.

- Language and culture: Arabic first, with a right-to-left layout.

- Access: it runs in a browser with nothing to install.

- Engagement: levels, points and shuffled quiz answers so that students learn and do not memorize positions.

- Growth: every level uses the same template, so new artifacts and languages are easy to add.
